list.listitem: Suspect hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) in patients with hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. C
If HUS is suspected, evaluate for antecedent infection by Shiga toxin-producing organisms or invasive Streptococcus pneumoniae, depending on the clinical presentation. C
Careful IV volume expansion and electrolyte management are the cornerstones of therapy for most cases. B

For patients with atypical HUS (aHUS), complement blockade, anti-C5 monoclonal antibody (eculizumab or ravulizumab) is considered first-line therapy; plasma exchange is suggested for patients with aHUS caused by anti-CFH or if the complement inhibitor is unavailable. B
Prevention and control measures should target reduction of foodborne and person-to-person transmission of Escherichia coli (E. coli) O157:H7 and other Shiga toxin-producing organisms. C
Mortality has improved from 30% to less than 10% with improved disease recognition and management; prognosis appears poorer for patients with aHUS. C
Death or end-stage renal disease (ESRD) occur in approximately 12% of patients, and 25% of patients have some evidence of long-term renal sequelae. C

HUS is characterized by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MTA), thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. The syndrome can be divided into two principal subgroups: typical cases with a diarrheal prodrome (D+ HUS) and atypical cases without an antecedent diarrheal illness (D− HUS). HUS can also be classified as primary (typical or atypical) or secondary (with a coexisting disease such as infection, transplantation, cancer, and autoimmune disease).

A greater understanding of the causes of HUS has led to a new classification system including infectious causes (most common), disorders of complement regulation (genetic and acquired aHUS), ADAMTS13 abnormalities (a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with a thrombospondin type 1 motif, member 13), defective cobalamine metabolism (quinine-induced, aHUS), and unknown etiology (e.g., associated with HIV, malignancy, drugs [e.g., antiplatelet agents, chemotherapy agents, vascular endothelial growth factor inhibitors], pregnancy, systemic lupus erythematosus).
The annual incidence is 1.4 per 100,000 persons per year, with approximately 90% of cases occurring after a diarrheal prodrome.
In Europe and North America, the annual incidence in children aged 3-5 years is 1.9-2.9/100,000 and for children <15-18 years, 0.6-0.8/100,000.
In a French surveillance study of children, HUS incidence rate was 1.0/100,000 children-years, with a median of 116 cases/year.
Based on cohort studies, 7.8% of participants with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli and 8% of participants with Shigella dysenteriae type 1 developed HUS during follow-up.

Among 927 children infected with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, 41 (4.4%) had HUS at presentation and 126 (14.2%) developed HUS. Predictors of HUS development included younger age (0.77 per year), leukocyte count ≥13.0 × 103/μL (2.54), higher hematocrit (1.83 per 5% increase) and serum creatinine (10.82 per 1 mg/dL increase), platelet count <250 × 103/μL (1.92), lower serum sodium (1.12 per 1 mmol/L decrease), and intravenous fluid (IV) administration initiated ≥4 days following diarrhea onset (2.50).
The incidence of aHUS is about 5% that of typical HUS. Estimated incidence of aHUS is 0.23-0.42 cases per million population.

Based on a systematic review of aHUS from France, Norway, Australia, and Italy, the annual incidence among those aged 20 years or younger ranged from 0.26 to 0.75 per million population; for all ages, annual incidence was 0.23 to 1.9 per million population.

In the 4-country systematic review noted above, prevalence of aHUS among those aged 20 years or younger was 2.2 to 9.4 per million population; based on a single study, prevalence of aHUS for all age groups was 4.9 per million population.

In a retrospective analysis of patients with aHUS treated with eculizumab and identified through a hospital database, estimated total hospital costs (year 2017 values) were $103,557 in late initiators of eculizumab and $85,776 in early initiators of the drug. Late initiators were 3.2 times more likely to require dialysis but there were no significant associations between early initiation and time to discharge, readmission, or death.
HUS due to Shiga toxin-producing E. coli is the leading cause of acute renal failure in young children in France.

In a study of 292 household contacts of 82 children with HUS related to Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, over one third (36.6%) had positive household contacts - 14 (38.8%) were children, 20 were adults, and 2 were dogs. One sibling developed HUS, 6 contacts had gastrointestinal symptoms, and the remainder were asymptomatic.

D+ HUS follows a diarrheal illness due to Shiga toxin-producing organisms such as Shigella dysenteriae and, more commonly, strains of E. coli, particularly E. coli O157:H7. Contact with farm animals is a risk factor for development of HUS after contracting Shiga toxin-producing E. coli. In a case series of 784 patients with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, 46 (6%) developed HUS and 24 (52%) of them reported direct contact with farm animals vs. 21% of those who did not developed HUS.

The use of antimotility agents in the setting of E. coli O157:H7 has been shown to increase the risk of D+ HUS. Studies evaluating the impact of antibiotic therapy in cases of E. coli O157:H7 on the outcome of D+ HUS have been conflicting, however. Because antibiotics likely prolong the duration of diarrheal illness, use of antibiotics in this setting is discouraged.

D− HUS is a heterogeneous group of disorders associated with nondiarrheal Shiga toxin-producing E. coli infections such as UTI, invasive pneumococcal disease, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, genetic or acquired deficiencies in complement components (aHUS), most notably factor H, malignancy, and drugs, including multiple immunosuppressive and chemotherapeutic agents. Viral infections, including adenovirus, can also lead to HUS.
Streptococcus pneumonia-associated HUS is responsible for 5% to 15% of HUS cases.
Atypical HUS is caused by uncontrolled complement activation in the alternative pathway.

Genetic susceptibility to aHUS has been demonstrated. About 60% involve mutations in complement C3 or in the inhibitory complement regulator factor H. In a report of a post-partum woman with aHUS, two missense variants of CD46 were identified that resulted in impairment in degradation of C3b. One case was reported of a novel genetic point mutation of complement factor H gene (p.Gly1110Ala) mimicking secondary HUS with scleroderma. No mutation is identified in 30% to 50%.
Atypical HUS following aortic valve replacement has been reported.
Causes of HUS share a common final pathway of thrombosis and inflammation of the endothelial cell surface.

After ingestion of food or water contaminated with Shiga toxin-producing organisms, exotoxin enters the intestinal circulation and travels in plasma on the surface of neutrophils. Exotoxin then binds to endovascular cells via globotriosyl ceramide (Gb3) receptors to initiate the formation of platelet-rich thrombi in the microvasculature of affected organs, particularly the kidney.

When studied in vitro, disruption of energy metabolism and depletion of glutathione contributed to Shiga toxin-induced renal endothelium injury with alteration of the nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide cofactor pathway and the inflammation-modulating eicosanoid pathway; the inflammatory response was found to be highly cell-type specific. Complement hyperactivation also appears to be a pathogenetic factor in various types of infection-induced HUS.
The resultant microangiopathy leads to fragmentation of erythrocytes and ischemia of involved organs.

Human cells susceptible to Shiga toxin-mediated injury are endothelial cells, proximal tubular epithelial cells, mesangial cells, podocytes, intestinal epithelial cells, and monocytes/macrophages and, once injured, these cells secrete inflammatory cytokines and chemokines such as tumor necrosis factor-α interleukin (IL)-1, IL-6, and IL-8.

In aHUS, patients develop thrombotic microangiopathy attributable in most cases to mutations that lead to activation of the alternative pathway of complement. Inability of abnormal FH molecules to simultaneously bind sialic acid and C3b on cells may explain the onset of aHUS in cases due to factor H inhibition. Differentiating between genetically-driven vs. time-limited complement storm-mediated aHUS has treatment implications.

In cases of S. pneumonia-associated HUS, the production of neuraminidase by the bacteria results in Thomsen-Friedenreich antigen exposure that can result in hemolysis and direct endothelial injury, leading to the HUS phenotype. In addition, the bacteria have been shown to bind human plasminogen via bacterial surface proteins and the activated protease degrades fibrinogen and cleaves C3b.

In a screening study from Italy of stool samples from 2.3 million children with bloody diarrhea, 214 (4.5%) were positive for either Shiga toxin 1 (29.0%), Shiga toxin 2 (45.3%) or both (25.7%). None of the children with stool samples positive for Shiga toxin 1 alone developed D+HUS compared to those with Shiga toxin 2 alone (27%) or Shiga toxin 1 and/or 2 (12.7%).
Prevention and control measures should target reduction of foodborne and person-to-person transmission of E. coli O157:H7 and other Shiga toxin-producing organisms. C

Authors of a Cochrane review evaluating antibiotics, bovine milk, and Shiga toxin inhibitor (Synsorb Pk) and monoclonal antibodies (Urtoxazumab) against Shiga toxin for secondary prevention of HUS in patients with diarrhea due to Shiga toxin-producing E. coli were unable to determine benefit due to the small number of included studies and the small sample sizes.

In a small case series, daily bowel lavage with polyethylene glycol solution reduced the incidence of HUS following Shiga toxin-producing enterohemorrhagic E. coli O104:H4 infection from 8/12 patients who did not receive lavage to 4/21 patients who received lavage.

In kidney transplantation patients with aHUS, use of eculizumab, a C5-complement inhibitor, is associated with a reduced likelihood of aHUS recurrence (odds ratio [OR] 0.05, 95% CI 0.00-0.13), as well as a significant reduction in need for dialysis (OR 0.13, 95% CI: 0.01-0.32) based on a meta-analysis including 18 trials with 618 subjects (see Management of Complications below). B
Suspect HUS in patients with hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. C
Low platelets do not appear to be a necessary criterion; one group of authors found that 13% of 150 patients with HUS had normal platelet counts.
If HUS is suspected, perform a careful history and laboratory evaluation for antecedent infection by a Shiga toxin-producing organism. C
Laboratory evidence of minimal coagulation activation and the absence of secondary fibrinolysis help distinguish HUS from disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). C

As differentiation of HUS from thrombotic thrombocytopenia purpura has implications for management and prognosis; emerging diagnostic testing strategies such as ADAMTS13 assays and a 9-analyte complement serology panel may prove valuable. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Prerenal disease; absence of thrombocytopenia and hemolytic anemia
Rash and arthralgias typically present; normal platelet count and coagulation studies
Evidence of coagulation activation and secondary fibrinolysis
Rash and arthralgias common; neurological manifestations more likely peripheral
Precedent hypertension; papilledema and retinal hemorrhages on examination
More common/severe CNS involvement; less significant renal insufficiency

list.listitem: In a retrospective review of 76 children, patients with D+ HUS presented with a prodromal illness that consisted of bloody diarrhea (80% of cases), emesis (80%), abdominal pain/tenderness (60%), and fever (33%).
Subsequent signs and symptoms of HUS depend on specific organ involvement and severity of disease but may include irritability, pallor, peripheral edema, and a petechial rash.
Hypertension is present in 15% to 60% of patients on presentation.

CNS involvement, mainly seizure and stupor, was observed in 25% of patients in one prospective surveillance study of 394 patients with HUS. Authors of a meta-analysis of 21 studies including 2,189 participants of median age between 1.3 and 40 years found rates of neurologic complications of 27% (95% CI 22.0%-32.6%) in those with D+HUS and 20.8% (95% CI 17.9%-24.0%) in those with D-HUS. Of patients with neurologic complications, seizures were reported in 20.8% of those with D+HUS and 30.5% with D-HUS. Other neurologic complications reported with D-HUS included coma (17.5%), speech abnormalities (7.4%), visual-disturbances (6.4%) and hemiparesis (5.6%).
Pancreatic injury (20% of cases), with or without endocrine insufficiency, as well as rare cardiac dysfunction can also occur.

In one German study of 106 patients with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli-associated HUS admitted to eight ICUs, the median time from onset of clinical symptoms to hospital admission was 3 days and from hospital to ICU admission was an additional 3 days.

S. pneumonia-HUS follows episodes of severe S. pneumonia sepsis. In a retrospective study of 9 patients with nonenteric S. pneumoniae associated HUS, 1 patient had meningitis and the others had pneumonia. The mean durations of anemia and thrombocytopenia were 19.2 and 10.2 days, respectively. All had hypertension and 5 patients, including the one with meningitis, experienced CNS complications.

In a case series of 45 patients with aHUS associated with anti-FH autoantibody, most cases were children between 9 and 13 years old. There was a high frequency of GI symptoms and extrarenal complications, and the clinical course was relapsing.

A diagnosis of HUS is supported by laboratory evidence of hemolysis (elevated lactate dehydrogenase [LDH], decreased hemoglobin with or without schistocytes on peripheral smear), thrombocytopenia (<150,000/μL or a decline of >25% compared with the baseline), and intrinsic renal failure.
Stool and urine cultures in cases of D- HUS, should be sent to assess for Shiga toxin-producing organisms.
Thrombocytopenia is rarely so severe as to cause bleeding, with platelet counts less than 20 × 109 cells/L observed in fewer than 20% of cases.
An elevated neutrophil count at presentation is a poor prognostic feature.

HUS can be differentiated from DIC by the absence of marked laboratory signs of coagulation activation and secondary fibrinolysis, including low levels of fibrinogen and coagulation factors V and VIII as well as the presence of fibrin degradation products in the serum. Prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) will be prolonged and D-dimer elevated in DIC.
Use von Willebrand factor cleaving protease (ADAMTS13) activity, antigen, and autoantibody assays to differentiate HUS from thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) .

An expert panel of Critical Care Physicians recommend the following for diagnosing aHUS: To establish presence of thrombotic microangiopathy - reticulocyte count, free serum hemoglobin, lactate dehydrogenase, serum creatinine (all elevated); haptoglobin, platelet count, hemoglobin (all decreased) and presence of schistocytes on peripheral smear and hematuria/proteinuria. Additional tests to rule out other causes of thrombotic microangiopathy - Coombs test (positive in autoimmune hemolytic anemia and pneumococcal HUS); fibrinogen, PT, aPTT, D-dimer, plasma coagulation tests (normal in aHUS and indicative of DIC); liver enzyme levels (can be elevated but elevated in HELLP); viral infections (HIV, hepatitis B and C, H1N1 – can precipitate aHUS); antibody testing (antinuclear antibody, lupus anticoagulant, antiphospholipid antibodies [normal in HUS]); stool or rectal swab for enterotoxins and ADAMTS13 activity (>10% in aHUS).

In patients presenting with features of aHUS, the British guideline recommends assessing serum levels of C3, C4, factor H and factor H autoantibodies, factor I, ADAMTS13 activity, and expression of CD46 on PBMCs, the latter using FACS analysis in an appropriately accredited laboratory as the results guide prognosis and late transplantation options. In addition, mutation screening of CFH, CD46, CFI, CFB and C3 is recommended.

The European Paediatric Study Group for HUS suggests the above tests in addition to homocysteine, methylmalonic acid (plasma and urine) ± mutation analysis in MMACHC gene (cobalamin metabolism), HIV serology, antinuclear antibody, lupus anticoagulant, anti-phospholipid antibodies and, if possibly pregnant, a pregnancy test and liver enzymes (HELLP syndrome—hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelet count).

A 9-analyte complement serology panel covering complement function (CH50 and AH50), components (C3, C4), factor B (CFB), factor H, and activation markers (C4d, Bb, and soluble membrane attack complex) may be useful in diagnosing aHUS. In one study, a combined factor B of 20.9 mg/dL or less and CH50 of 56% or less led to sensitivity of 75%, specificity of 88.9%, and a diagnostic OR of 24 for aHUS.

Use of the automated fragmented red blood cell (FRC) percentage was examined in 28 pediatric patients with HUS. In children with an FRC% >1.49%, sensitivity was 95.4% (95% CI 77.16% to 99.88%) and specificity was 50% (95% CI 11.81% to 88.19%) with a positive likelihood ratio of 1.9 and area under the curve of 0.84.
A rapid, serum-based assay that helps to differentiate aHUS from other thrombotic microangiopathies is under development.

Authors of a study of 15 patients with aHUS and 20 with secondary thrombotic microangiopathy found that no test showed a significant difference between these groups and 3 patients with aHUS patients met DIC criteria.
See for a suggested approach to management.

The expert-based guideline from the European Paediatric Study Group for HUS suggests assigning cases of recognized HUS into three clinical presentations—D+ HUS in those older than 6 months of age residing in an area endemic for enterohemorrhagic E. coli or Shigella dysenteriae type 1 (likely Shiga toxin-induced infectious HUS); patients with invasive S. pneumoniae including cases of pneumonia, meningitis, and/or septicemia, especially if there is loculated infection (e.g., empyema) (likely pneumococcus-induced infectious HUS); and other HUS cases.
The infectious categories require bacteriological confirmation and treatment including antibiotics and supportive care.
The other HUS cases require full work-up, as noted above, and consideration of complement blockade and/or plasma exchange.
Careful IV volume expansion and electrolyte management are the cornerstones of therapy. B
The role of antibiotics for Shiga toxin-producing E. coli strains is evolving. C
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are the agent of choice for management of chronic and perhaps acute hypertension. B
Consider packed red blood cell transfusion for symptomatic anemia, with platelet transfusion reserved for rare cases involving severe thrombocytopenia and bleeding. C
For patients with aHUS, terminal complement inhibition appears to offer improved outcomes, based upon very low-quality evidence. B
Plasma infusion has not been shown to improve outcomes, and therapeutic plasma exchange should only be considered in cases of D− HUS or D+ HUS with severe CNS manifestations. C

With respect to antibiotic use for Shiga toxin-producing E. coli strains, authors of a review found beta-lactams and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole to be detrimental with respect to development of HUS, while fosfomycin appeared to have the most positive results from clinical studies for averting HUS development, especially if administered within the first 2 to 3 days from diarrhea onset. Fluoroquinolones also showed positive outcomes in clinical studies and other agents (e.g., colistin, gentamycin and rifamycins) require further study.
ACE inhibitors may be used in the acute setting to treat hypertension.

A comparative study of 45 subjects with HUS-induced renal disease suggested that patients who were treated with ACE inhibitors had better long-term outcome of renal function than those maintained on other antihypertensive agents.

A very small pilot study randomized 10 patients with HUS to erythropoietin plus standard therapy or standard therapy alone. There was a decreased need for red blood cell transfusions in the treated group, but safety and clinical efficacy evaluation will require a larger trial.

For patients with aHUS, authors of a Cochrane review of 5 single-arm trials concluded that terminal complement inhibition appears to offer improved outcomes, based upon very low-quality evidence at high risk of bias. In the 3 primary and one secondary study of eculizumab, including 137 patients, there were no deaths and a 70% reduction in the number of patients requiring dialysis after 26 weeks. Complete thrombotic microangiopathic (TMA) response was observed in 60% of patients at 26 weeks and 65% at two years. In the single study of ravulizumab with 58 participants, at 26 weeks, complete response was seen in 54% and 4 patients died. Serious adverse events occurred in 42% of patients, including meningococcal infection which occurred in two patients on eculizumab.

Based on 9 case reports or case series and one clinical trial, adverse infectious consequences resulting from use of eculizumab included invasive meningococcal disease, N. gonorrhoeae infection, unusual Neisseria species infection, P. aeruginosa, and Moraxella lacunata infection.

Authors of a review of 16 reports concluded that eculizumab resulted in clinical improvement in patients with severe Shiga toxin-producing E. coli -HUS with progressive neurological involvement based on low-quality evidence.
Rituximab and plasmapheresis were used successfully in an adult with anti-factor H autoantibody-associated aHUS.

A potential new therapy for HUS is thrombomodulin, an endothelial membrane protein that has anticoagulation and anti-inflammatory effects, including the suppression of complement activity. Recombinant human soluble thrombomodulin resulted in recovery of three patients with HUS.

With respect to kidney transplantation, recurrence of HUS in the allograft is seen in about half of patients with HUS overall, but is much less frequent in patients with CD46 mutation, but no additional mutations. The British guideline recommends consideration of isolated liver or combined liver/kidney transplant within a clinical trial for a patient with aHUS with a known mutation in either CFH or CFI.
Careful IV volume expansion and electrolyte management are the cornerstones of therapy.
Packed red blood cell transfusion should be considered for symptomatic anemia. Platelet transfusion is rarely required unless there is active bleeding or need for an invasive procedure.

Prospective studies have shown no apparent benefit from treatment with plasma infusion, whereas a retrospective study of therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) suggested benefit but was of limited quality.

Patients with D−HUS, particularly those with familial forms, are often considered for TPE, although data supporting this approach are limited. TPE should be considered in patients with severe CNS involvement and/or fever where differentiation from TTP on clinical grounds may be difficult. In a meta-analysis of three trials in adults with HUS, there was no difference in outcomes between plasma exchange using cryo-supernatant plasma or plasma exchange using fresh frozen plasma.

The expert panel recommends initiating plasma therapy within 4-8 hours of admission with a diagnosis of TMA but switching to eculizumab if a diagnosis of aHUS is confirmed (ADAMS13>10% and negative shiga toxin-producing E. coli).

Both older guidelines for aHUS recommend plasma exchange as first-line therapy while diagnostic testing is pursued, although supporting data are limited. Exceptions to this include cases where an alternate treatment is available based on diagnosis (e.g., congenital ADAMTS13 deficiency; cobalamin-C disorder in a child with failure to thrive, hypotonia, leukopenia and megaloblastic anemia; cases where difficulties in vascular access are present; or where the risks outweigh benefits in a child with mild renal involvement).

Authors of a Cochrane review identified 7 RCTs of children with HUS, including studies of fresh frozen plasma transfusion, heparin with or without urokinase or dipyridamole, shiga toxin binding protein and steroids, and found none of these superior to supportive therapy with regard to any clinical outcomes. More patients receiving anticoagulants bled (RR 26; 95% CI, 3.7-182).

Authors of a case report and literature review caution that discontinuing eculizumab may risk recurrence of thrombotic microangiopathy particularly in patients with complement factor H mutations. Risk of recurrence appears low in patients with MCP mutations, homozygous CFHR3/R1 deletions, anti-CFH antibodies, CFI mutations, and in those with no identifiable mutations.

Relapse occurs in 20% to 35% of patients with aHUS following eculizumab cessation after a median of 3 months (range, 1-30 months). One author of a review concluded that eculizumab may be discontinued in some groups of patients on a case-by-case basis and with careful monitoring, following 6 to 12 months of treatment for aHUS that encompasses at least 3 months of normalization of renal function or stabilization of chronic renal disease.

In a prospective national multicenter open-label study with 55 patients with aHUS, 13 patients (23%; 6 children and 7 adults) experienced an aHUS relapse following discontinuation of eculizumab. Risk factors for relapse were female sex, presence of a rare variant in a complement gene and increased sC5b-9 plasma level at eculizumab discontinuation. Reinstitution of eculizumab in these 13 patients resulted in 11 regaining their baseline renal function; two had a worsening of their preexisting chronic kidney disease, including 1 patient who progressed to end-stage renal disease.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 cohort studies and 5 case series with 380 adult kidney transplant patients with aHUS investigated the role of eculizumab in preventing recurrent atypical HUS and allograft loss. Of those who received eculizumab for prevention, incidence rates for recurrence were low at 6.3% (95%CI: 2.8-13.4%) as was allograph loss (5.5%; 95%CI: 2.9-10.0%). Among those treated with eculizumab for post-transplant aHUS recurrence, the pooled estimated rate of allograft loss was 22.5% (95%CI 13.6-34.8%).
Mortality has improved from 30% to less than 10% with improved disease recognition and management; prognosis appears poorer for patients with aHUS. C
Initial significant leukocytosis, severe CNS involvement, and persistent proteinuria beyond 1 year portend a worse prognosis. C
Death or ESRD occurs in approximately 12% of patients, and 25% of patients have some evidence of long-term renal sequelae. C
A retrospective analysis of 67 cases of HUS from 1962 to 1969, prior to significant advances in disease management, demonstrated an overall mortality rate of 34%.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 49 studies with 3476 patients found that death or ESRD occurs in about 12% of patients with D+ HUS.

In the German study of 106 ICU patients with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli-associated HUS, the mortality rate was 4.7%. About three quarters of the patients required renal replacement therapy and about one third required intubation and mechanical ventilation. Almost half developed sepsis and, of these, one quarter developed septic shock. Sixty-six percent developed severe neurological symptoms. The median ICU stay was 10 days (range, 1-45 days).
Severe CNS involvement was associated with greater likelihood of mortality or ESRD.

In a follow-up study of adults with shiga-toxin associated HUS, at 19 months, 31 of the original 44 were available for follow-up revealing that 22 still suffered from symptoms such as fatigue, headache, and attention deficits and only 39% performed normally on neuropsychological assessments.

Among 770 children hospitalized with D+ HUS in 10 states during 1997 to 2012, most had good outcomes with few deaths (2.9%) and few requiring persistent dialysis at discharge (52/716; 7.3%). During hospitalization, nearly all (92.6%) required transfusion and over half (430/761; 56.5%) required dialysis. At a mean follow-up of 4.4 years, 25% of patients had a glomerular filtration rate lower than 80 mL/min/1.73 m2, hypertension, or proteinuria.
While studies are inconclusive, it is generally suggested that D- HUS is associated with worse outcomes than D+ HUS.

In an Australian follow-up study of 14 children with atypical HUS, 10 required dialysis at first presentation, including two who died and three who did not recover renal function. Five children developed neurological complications and two had cardiac complications, most at disease onset. Relapse occurred within the first 12 months in all but one child who survived the initial episode. At one-year follow-up, 9 of the remaining 11 patients were dialysis dependent; one child was lost to follow-up. Thirteen kidneys were transplanted into 8 children, but the disease recurred in 8 kidneys, resulting in graft loss in seven. Three further deaths occurred 1.7, 6.7 and 16.1 years after initial presentation.

In a retrospective study of 9 patients with non-enteric HUS, the mean durations of hypertension in 5 patients with CNS manifestations and 4 patients without CNS manifestations were 16.8 ± 7.8 days and 4.8 ± 6.6 days, respectively. Two patients died in the acute stage; most others regained normal renal function at discharge or during follow-up.

In a case series of patients with aHUS associated with anti-FH autoantibody, patients showing activation of the alternative pathway of complement at the onset of disease had a poorer prognosis. In another case series of patients with aHUS and renal transplant, mutations in complement genes, identified in 68%, were associated with higher risk of recurrence.

A meta-analysis of 10 studies with 159 renal allografts in 127 patients demonstrated an HUS recurrence rate of 27.8% in patients who had previously received renal allograft; older age at onset of HUS (presumably representing a greater proportion of D− HUS) was associated with recurrence.
Patients should be monitored for signs of hypertension, proteinuria, and evidence of persistent renal dysfunction.
Persistent proteinuria after 1 year may be associated with increased risk for progressive renal disease.

Authors of a systematic review of pregnancy-associated aHUS found 48 reports describing 60 unique cases with 66 pregnancies. The diagnosis most often occurred postpartum (94%), after a cesarean delivery (70%), and in nulliparous women (58%). For women with first-episode pregnancy-associated aHUS, treatment with eculizumab achieved a higher rate of disease remission compared to no treatment with eculizumab (88% vs 57%, respectively).

Ravulizumab was investigated in 8 patients, 5 of whom were on dialysis at baseline, who developed TMA post-partum and were diagnosed with aHUS. Complete TMA response was achieved in 7/8 patients (87.5%) in a median time of 31.5 days. Hematologic normalization was observed in all patients and the 5 patients on dialysis discontinued dialysis within 21 days after treatment with ravulizumab. Possible treatment-related adverse events were observed in 2 patients (arthralgia and nasopharyngitis [both non-severe] and one with urinary tract infection).

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 cohort studies, 4 case series, and 1 clinical trial with 940 pediatric patients, 682 of whom received eculizumab, found consistent improvements in renal and hematological parameters in most patients treated with eculizumab with a mortality rate of 1.6% for treated patients.

In an RCT including 100 children with Shiga toxin-related HUS comparing 4 weeks of eculizumab to placebo, there were no differences in renal outcome during the acute disease phase (e.g., renal replacement therapy required in 38% and 48%, respectively), but those randomized to eculizumab had a reduced rate of long-term kidney sequelae at 1 year (43.5% and 64.4%, respectively).

Similarly, ravulizumab was effective for complete TMA response at 26 weeks in 77.8% of 18 children with aHUS and in 94.4% at 50 weeks of treatment in a phase III, single-arm trial. Ravulizumab was administered every eight weeks in patients 20 kg and over, and four weeks in patients under 20 kg. No deaths or meningococcal infections occurred.

A prospective study of 29 children with D+ HUS demonstrated that later initiation of IV volume expansion was associated with a higher risk of oligoanuric renal failure. Early volume expansion (soon after diagnosis) was also found beneficial in a case series of children with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli-associated HUS compared to historical controls in terms of less central nervous system involvement, less need for renal replacement therapy or intensive care support, fewer days of hospitalization and longer-term renal and extrarenal sequelae.
In a pilot RCT with 24 children with HUS related to Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, there was no benefit of recombinant human erythropoietin on number of RBC transfusions.
Indications for renal dialysis are similar to those in children with other forms of renal failure.
